scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the Aymara cosmology of Puno, the dance celebrates a moment of equilibrium between the forces of the underworld and the heavens, marking the point when the world began to advance.
This is Diablada puneña. 16th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Diablada puneña · Peru · 16th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the 16th century among the Lupaka people in Puno, influenced by Jesuit missionaries who used theater to evangelize.
It evolved from the ancient Aymara dance of the Anchanchu and was later consolidated through the cult of the Virgin of the Candelaria.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is performed at major religious festivals such as the Festividad de la Virgen de la Candelaria in Puno and the feast of the Immaculate Conception in Juli, representing the struggle between good and evil.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features a confrontation between angels and demons.
Dancers perform in groups, with the Caporal leading the devils.
Movements include jumps and aggressive steps, with the devils using tridents to clear a path for the musicians.
Watch for Devil's march.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Group formations, often in streets or plazas.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally accompanied by sikuris (panpipes), the modern Diablada puneña uses the 'sicu-moreno' ensemble, which includes sikus, bass drums, snare drums, cymbals, and triangles, playing syncopated huaynos.
Listen for the sikus, bombo, tambor redoblante, platillos.
A driving, syncopated rhythm led by panpipes (sikus) and supported by a percussion section of bass drums, snare drums, and triangles.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear elaborate masks (formerly plaster, now metal or other materials) featuring horns and reptilian motifs.
Angels wear wings and swords, while devils wear capes and masks representing the seven deadly sins.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include the Jesuit father Diego González Holguín, who introduced early theatrical forms, and mask-makers Alberto and Ramón Velásquez, who established workshops in 1956.
The Diablada puneña is distinct from the Bolivian Diablada due to its unique musical accompaniment (sicu-moreno) and specific historical development in the Puno region.
It is a descendant of the ancient Anchanchu dance and the colonial-era autos sacramentales.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is deeply tied to Aymara cosmology and Catholic religious festivals; it is a ritual performance and should be observed with respect during religious processions.
